This Course has been a mistake for students of International Relations. It has been a mistake to offer a course for students of political science and international relations together, especially when instructor himself has a background of political science. These two fields are totally different in their methodology. Also, the content of course or nature of given examples were all borrowed from political science. For IR students, it is important to analyze interstate relations, not the domestic environment of states. Therefore, course content failed to address important methodological tools to conduct research on relations between two-or-more states, or how to analyze them historically. The course also failed to explain 'case study' methodology which is very crucial for IR research. I do not blame an instructor Tolga hoca but I it was the fault of administration to assign political science instructor for IR students. Due to all these failures, I consider taking this course again next semester because methodlogy is crucial to conduct of master thesis. Hope next year, there will IR instructor, more emphasize on widely used IR methodologies, and more examples from IR world, and IR articles from research design.

The strongest aspect of the course is that it continually revisits and reconstructs concepts we think we already understand, pushing us to interrogate our assumptions and think more critically about research design. In doing so, it actively guides students to design, refine, and, when necessary, reformulate their research process in a more rigorous and self-aware manner.

Also, the idea of implementing a colloquium component was excellent, and I personally benefited a great deal from it. It was highly productive, effective, and appropriately challenging in a constructive way.

The main weakness is that, given the conceptual complexity and precision required, it would benefit from more systematic, weekly checks for understanding. For instance, short Moodle-based questions or brief weekly assignments, followed by an in-class explanation or an answer key, could reduce ambiguity and consolidate learning. A particularly challenging feature of the course is that one can feel confident about a concept, only to realise several weeks later that it was understood differently than intended. While quizzes and larger assignments are valuable, more consistent weekly feedback loops could help identify misunderstandings earlier and improve clarity over time.

The strongest aspect is that, even though the course load is high, it does a good job of equipping you with the necessary skills to read any academic publication with a technical eye and to apply those same skills while attempting to craft your own social research. The weakest aspect is the issue of student presentations that take place during the second half of the semester. Performance fluctuated according to the students’ level of comprehension of already difficult and very difficult research design techniques. This also created a chain effect on other students’ levels of comprehension, although the instructor intervened and supplemented the presentations at certain points.

Strong points: The instructor was very motivating from the beginning and was able to inspire (I would say almost all of his) students for a rather “dry”, demanding and very specific class. Complex topics about social economy and welfare states were very well-explained in proper and good English. Furthermore, his way of teaching contributed to the motivation of the students who participated on a high level and asked many questions which were always answered. Despite a clear course structure and high expectations, he was always interested in the needs and wishes of his students. He did not use many demotivating and pressuring control mechanisms as other Bilkent instructors used to do, such as doing weekly quizzes or penalizing students for not doing the readings every time. Instead, he trusts his students in doing their work, gives them student autonomy and encourages them to actively participate. Furthermore, he made sure that no student was left behind. Eventually, his flexible, compromising and student-friendly nature benefited my interest, motivation and learning effect.

Weaker points: The instructors' flexibility had on the other side the "weakness" of changing/adjusting the curriculum, making it more difficult to plan deadlines and other things. Besided this, I have some didactic preferences which I answered in the next survey question.
course:
Strong points: The course was content-wise very well-structured and logical, making it easy to follow the overall compley topic. The readings were a good of mix of old and new theories and concepts, giving a very comprehensive overview of the whole topic. The mix of graduate and undergraduate students in the class was also beneficial. As I wrote in the previous question, the instructors' teaching style and ability to explain things very well and enthusiastically, was one of the strongest points in this course. The course had a comfortable combination of high expectations and a welcoming/comfortable feeling in class. Despite a full front-of-class teaching method within a theoretical and demanding class, it was baerly boring or hard to follow the class.

Weaker points: Although I like front-of-class teaching, some different didactic elements might be useful, such as watching videos about the topic (in so far they exist), arranging group work or adding other exam performances other than classic essays, exams, presentations. This could be for instance creating scientific posters, podcasts, or panel discussions in order to teach them soft-skills which are useful in all sorts of future jobs in this field. Also, the overly structured essays and predetermined topics for the workshop presentations might prevent some students from developing their own research interest and learning effects in structuring scientific papers/essays themselves.
